extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature/poetics and creative writers interested in Aristotelian theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles from Aristotle's Poetics and a scholarly exposition: guidance for composing/evaluating poetry and drama (esp. tragedy vs epic), focusing on imitation, unity, plausibility, character, and the artful use of sensory elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for probable impossibility over possible improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: “A probable impossibility is to be preferred to a thing improbable and yet possible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet may present ideals or impossibilities if they are more likely to produce the proper aesthetic effect than a mere possible event that strains belief. Justification may appeal to received opinion or to the ideal type; the irrational can be allowed if it does not violate reason (cf. ‘it is probable that a thing may happen contrary to probability’).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine apparent contradictions by dialectical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: “Things that sound contradictory should be examined by the same rules as in dialectical refutation—whether the same thing is meant, in the same relation, and in the same sense.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve seeming contradictions by close attention to what the poet actually says or to what is tacitly assumed by an intelligent reader; do not dismiss elements as contradictory without this analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrational or depraved elements require inner necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The element of the irrational, and, similarly, depravity of character, are justly censured when there is no inner necessity for introducing them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting irrational incidents or morally depraved character traits unless they are essential to the plot or to the psychological truth of the work. Examples cited: the irrational introduction of Aegeus by Euripides; the badness of Menelaus in the Orestes—these are criticisms because they lack inner necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five common grounds for criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: “Things are censured either as impossible, or irrational, or morally hurtful, or contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or revising a work, anticipate objections under these five heads and supply answers (Aristotle suggests answers should be sought under his twelve heads elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate art by the refinement of its intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the more refined art is the higher, and the more refined in every case is that which appeals to the better sort of audience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider who the work is addressed to; an art that presumes a cultivated audience (requiring less gesture or explanatory padding) is viewed as more refined and higher. Audience sophistication is a criterion in ranking modes (e.g., epic vs tragedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of action/gesture (histrionic vs poetic art)
rubrics_metrics.description: “This censure attaches not to the poetic but to the histrionic art; for gesticulation may be equally overdone in epic recitation... Next, all action is not to be condemned—any more than all dancing—but only that of bad performers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge stage action and gesture by necessity and taste: only excessive or inappropriate physicality (often the fault of performers) should be censured. A text should be capable of producing its effect even without excessive gesture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy’s superiority via concentrated unity and vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is superior because it contains epic elements, can use music and spectacle, produces vivid pleasures, and attains its end within narrower limits—concentrated effect is more pleasurable than a long, diluted one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concentrated unity (single action) and vividness; excessive length spread over many parts can dilute the aesthetic effect. A tragedy should deliver the pleasure proper to it through concentrated structure and vivid presentation (also effective in mere reading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action — prefer single, unified plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic imitation has less unity; many epic poems provide material for several tragedies. If a story is to have strict unity it must be concise; length implies some loss of unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct narrative around a single coherent action or tightly related series; avoid sprawling plots that fragment the imitation and weaken unity. If multiple actions are present, treat them so each attains magnitude while preserving an overall unity where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art imitates human life (objects of imitation: ἤθη, πάθη, πράξεις)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The actual objects of aesthetic imitation are threefold—ἤθη (character), πάθη (passions/emotions), πράξεις (actions).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus imitation on inward processes: moral dispositions, transient emotions, and meaningful actions that spring from will or thought. External events (landscape, animals) are secondary unless they heighten human interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate actions as inward processes, not merely external acts
rubrics_metrics.description: “The πρᾶξις that art seeks to reproduce is mainly an inward process, a psychical energy working outwards; deeds, incidents, events... included so far as these spring from an inward act of will, or elicit some activity of thought or feeling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray the inner motivations and psychological dynamics that give external events their aesthetic import. Avoid staging or listing external events without showing their inward causal life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works should be likenesses to appearances (aesthetic semblance) not abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: “A work of art is a likeness (ὁμοίωμα) or reproduction of an original... Art addresses itself not to the abstract reason but to the sensibility and image-making faculty; it is concerned with outward appearances; it employs illusions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create convincing sensory/imagistic representation—the work should feel true in its appearances even if it does not express the abstract truth. Use illusion and vivid particulars to produce an aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain plausibility (τὸ πιθανόν) in internal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: “The doctrine of aesthetic semblance and of τὸ πιθανόν... the poet working by illusions ‘ought to prefer probable impossibilities to possible improbabilities.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure internal coherence and plausibility within the fiction's world; readers accept ideal or impossible facts if they feel probable within the work’s logic, but will reject scenarios that are merely possible yet feel implausible or arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on human interest—landscape and animals are background
rubrics_metrics.description: “The common original, then, from which all the arts draw is human life... On this principle landscape and animals are not ranked among the objects of aesthetic imitation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize human mental life and actions as the center of artistic concern; use non-human elements only insofar as they serve to heighten human action or emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of music, rhythm, and spectacle as enhancers of character and vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and spectacle are important accessories; music was held to be the most ‘imitative’ art, reproducing character in rhythms and melodies; accessories produce the most vivid pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dramatic and lyrical composition, attend to rhythm, musicality, and sensory presentation to amplify mood and moral character. Consider how non-verbal elements (rhythm, cadence, sound) reflect or shape ethical tone and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each art must produce its proper pleasure (fit-to-end criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Each art ought to produce, not any chance pleasure, but the pleasure proper to it...”—the higher art is that which attains its end more perfectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define what pleasure or effect your chosen mode is meant to produce (e.g., tragic catharsis, epic grandeur) and shape form, length, unity, and devices to serve that end rather than incidental delights.
